content:
Every church that holds the New Testament holds the same 27 books today. For several centuries the churches did not agree on them. Writers of the time had a word for the books that some churches read and others doubted.

Six facts show which books were disputed, who disputed them and how long the dispute ran.

In the early fourth century Eusebius sorted books into the recognised, the disputed and the heretical. The disputed books were James, 2 Peter, Jude, and 2 and 3 John.[1]

Eusebius recorded that these five were still in question in his time.

The Syriac Peshito lacks it. Didymus the Blind said it "is not in the canon". Junilius, writing about 550, still records books in grades.[2]

The letter now stands in every church's list. Some churches still left it out in the fifth century.

The Muratorian fragment rejects a letter "to the Alexandrians" as forged in Paul's name, which Davidson takes to mean Hebrews. The African list in the Clermont manuscript puts Barnabas in its place. Augustine admits Hebrews "by the authority of the Oriental churches".[3]

The Western church counted fourteen letters of Paul at Carthage in 419. Hebrews had been accepted on the word of the East.

The list attributed to Laodicea, whose date is disputed, and the lists of Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nazianzus and Amphilochius leave it out. Nicephorus places it among the disputed books about 810.[4]

The Revelation stands in every church's New Testament now. Its place there was reached by the end of a long dispute.

Luther judged James "a right strawy epistle", judged Hebrews not apostolic, and doubted Jude and the Revelation. The Lutherans kept a division into books accepted by all and books that were spoken against, and the Calvinists dropped it.[5]

Calvin doubted that Paul wrote Hebrews and that Peter wrote 2 Peter, and he held both canonical.

Codex Sinaiticus, of the fourth century, adds Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas. Codex Alexandrinus, of the fifth, carries the letters of Clement.[6]

A reader of those codices saw books a modern Bible leaves out. A reader of other lists saw a shorter New Testament.

The bottom line

The list of 27 is the outcome of a dispute that ran from the second century to the Reformation, with the doubts strongest in the East and over a few books.

Davidson wrote in 1877 that "The question of the canon is not settled."[7] That is his own view. The record supports a plainer point: churches that now agree on the list reached it by different roads.

Notes

  1. Davidson, Canon, pp. 76 to 77. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.25. Davidson calls this class "disputed"; the Greek word is antilegomena.
  2. Davidson, Canon, pp. 75, 92 to 93 and 104. See the site's article on the second letter of Peter.
  3. Davidson, Canon, pp. 73, 74 to 75 and 95 to 96.
  4. Davidson, Canon, pp. 88 to 92 and 106. See the site's article on Revelation 22:18 and the canon.
  5. Davidson, Canon, pp. 108 to 111.
  6. Davidson, Canon, pp. 94 and 106.
  7. Davidson, Canon, p. 127. Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament: Its Origin, Development, and Significance (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987).
